thread.title: Apple (AAPL) 2nd Quarter Earnings: What to Expect

author: Richard Saintvilus
title: Apple (AAPL) 2nd Quarter Earnings: What to Expect
text:
Apple earnings (Shutterstock photo)
Will reports of weak iPhone X sales, and possibly reduced guidance, continue the recent slide in Apple ( AAPL ) shares, which have fallen more than 5% over the past three months?
Investors are bracing for these answers when the tech giant reports second quarter fiscal 2018 earnings results after the closing bell Tuesday. Apple is the only remaining FAANG — Facebook ( FB ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Netflix ( NFLX ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) — that have yet to report earnings. And investors who are willing to hold Apple for the next 12 to 18 months should use this pullback as a buying opportunity.
In the three months that ended March, Wall Street expect the company to report earnings per share of $2.69 on revenue of $60.98 billion. This compares to the year-ago quarter when Apple earned $2.10 per share on $52.9 billion in revenue. For the full year, ending October, earnings are expected to rise 23.7% year over year to $11.40 per share, while full-year revenue of $261.16 billion would rise 13.9% year over year.
On Tuesday all eyes will be on the performance of the iPhone X. Launched last fall at a price of $999, the device was a part of Apple’s super-cycle, drawing expectations of massive phone upgrades reminiscent of the iPhone 6’s success in 2015. That level of excitement sent Apple shares to all-time highs of $183.50. But the Cupertino-based company has since erased all of its year-to-date stock gains and is now down more than 4% on the year.
The reason? Citing negative supply-chain data, several analysts have warned that iPhone unit sales could disappoint for the just-completed quarter. Wall Street is looking for total Q2 iPhone unit sales of 53 million, which would mark a 15% decline from prior estimates of 62 million at the start of the quarter. The reduced expectations can work in Apple’s favor since the company has a lower bar to jump over.
What’s more, the fact that the stock has fallen as much as 12% to a recent low of $160 suggests the lowered iPhone unit sales is baked into the stock price. As such, it’s more important to focus on other areas of the business such as Services, which includes Apple Music, the App Store and Apple Pay. These have grown to become Apple's second-largest business, while delivering the highest profit margins. In Q1, Services revenue grew 18% year over year to $8.47 billion, topping forecasts of $8.05 billion.
Notably, despite a sizable miss on iPhone unit sales last quarter, the performance of the Services segment was the main reason Apple still topped the Street’s earnings and revenue targets in Q1. In other words, Apple is becoming gradually less dependent on the iPhone for its success. Therefore, investors would be better served to shift their focus on things like capital allocation and what the company plans to do with its massive cash stockpile such as increasing its buyback and raising its dividend.
